Finding a name

Can typo-tolerant search help students find a directory entry they can’t quite spell, while keeping correctly spelled searches predictable?

Audience and scope

The intended reader is a student testing a small directory lookup. The first slice searches a fixed set of fictional names in the browser. It can inform a later app where a student signs in, saves a result, returns to a private dashboard, and manages their account.

Assumptions to test. The directory is small enough for in-browser filtering. Students sometimes remember only part of a name or transpose letters. A plausible wrong match could send someone to the wrong record.

Two approaches

Normalized substring

Trim spaces, use lowercase and Unicode NFC, then look for the same character sequence inside each name. This is the baseline. Its behavior is easy to explain and reproduce, but it misses spelling errors.

Fuse.js fuzzy ranking

Score approximate matches and return the best candidates. It could recover misspellings. The ranking and score threshold need testing against similar names and queries with no intended match.

Decision. Keep literal matching as the first pass. Test fuzzy results only as a fallback when the baseline has no match, and label them as possible matches if the evaluation supports adopting it.

Baseline checks

Five fixed assertions ran locally on November 11, 2026. Each observed result agreed with the baseline expectation. The missed typo is an observed limitation that motivates the next experiment.

Four fictional names, five queries

Uppercase BEN PARK with spacesBen ParkBen Park
ChenAvery ChenAvery Chen

Results appear here.

Next experiment

Run both approaches on the same 12 labeled queries. Include four exact or partial names, five typos, and three queries with no intended match. Include two deliberately similar names. Keep the same fixture and record the returned names and order.

Proposed acceptance check. Add fuzzy suggestions only if at least four of five typos put the intended name in the top three, all four existing matches stay first, and no more than one of the three unrelated queries returns suggestions. The fuzzy comparison is pending.

Partner task. Try Chen and Jodran, then explain what would justify changing the behavior.

Sources and AI use

Technical references reviewed November 11, 2026.

  • The ECMAScript specification defines literal substring inclusion and Unicode normalization. These establish the baseline’s string operations. Substring inclusion · Unicode normalization
  • Fuse.js documents approximate matches, ranked results and searchable fields. Its examples establish the option’s behavior on the documentation examples. Fuse.js documentation

AI helped draft the comparison and fixture. The library and language claims were checked against their original documentation. The five baseline cases were executed separately. Ranking quality with this fixture and usefulness with students still need testing.
